explanations.answer: They had no opportunity to show it
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what Paul says. They were indeed concerned, but they had no opportunity to show it (Philippians 4:10). Caring and getting the chance to act on it are two different things, friend. I've had a whole batch of good intentions sitting in my head with no oven in sight.

explanations.answer: They didn't know where he was staying
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that. He says they were indeed concerned, but they had no opportunity to show it (Philippians 4:10). The text doesn't give a reason about an address. It just says the opportunity wasn't there, and the care was real the whole time.

explanations.answer: They were waiting for him to ask them
explanations.explanation: Nope, and Paul doesn't say anything about waiting for a request. He says they were indeed concerned, but they had no opportunity to show it (Philippians 4:10). Their care was there all along. The chance just hadn't come yet.

Content is the word. Paul says he has learned to be content regardless of his circumstances (Philippians 4:11). Notice the word "learned." He didn't wake up with it, friend. I'm still learning it myself, especially when a fresh batch is cooling right next to me.

Close in sound, far in meaning. Paul says he has learned to be content regardless of his circumstances (Philippians 4:11). Cautious is about watching your step. Content is about being settled in whatever step you're on.

Paul doesn't say silent, and honestly, a man who writes a whole letter from chains isn't trying to be quiet. He says he has learned to be content regardless of his circumstances (Philippians 4:11). Content means settled, not hushed.

Paul says the opposite of always having plenty. He says, "I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound." He's learned the secret of "being filled and being hungry, of having plenty and having need." (Philippians 4:12). It goes both directions, friend. The secret works in the full seasons and the empty ones.

Right, because the secret isn't about always having plenty. Paul says he has learned "the secret of being filled and being hungry, of having plenty and having need." (Philippians 4:12). He knows both sides of the counter. That's what makes his secret worth listening to.

explanations.answer: Through Christ who gives him strength
explanations.explanation: That's the one. "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength." (Philippians 4:13). The strength comes from Christ, and Paul says so plainly. It's right there in the verse, no gym wall needed.

explanations.answer: Through the friends who support him
explanations.explanation: The Philippians' support mattered to Paul, and he thanks them for it. But in this verse he says, "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength." (Philippians 4:13). The strength comes from Christ.

explanations.answer: Through Timothy who serves with him
explanations.explanation: Timothy, Paul's coworker, is a good man to have around (Philippians 2:19-22). But he's not who Paul names here. Paul says, "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength." (Philippians 4:13).

Affliction is it. Paul says, "you have done well to share in my affliction." (Philippians 4:14). They stepped into his hard season with him. I think that's the kind of friend who shows up when the oven's broken, not just when the cookies are done.
Paul doesn't say honors. He says they have done well to share in his affliction (Philippians 4:14). Sharing in the hard part is the whole point. Anybody can show up for the good stuff.
A fun word, but not Paul's. He says they have done well to share in his affliction (Philippians 4:14). He's writing from chains, so affliction is what's on the table. They joined him there.

None is right. Paul says when he left Macedonia, "no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving." (Philippians 4:15). Only the Philippians. Zero other churches, friend. That's a short list with one name on it.

Careful here. The one church is the Philippians themselves. Paul says, "no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving." (Philippians 4:15). So besides them, the number is none.

Not even close, friend. Paul says, "no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving." (Philippians 4:15). Besides the Philippians, no church did. That makes their giving stand out even more.

Again and again is right. Paul says that even in Thessalonica, "you provided for my needs again and again." (Philippians 4:16). Not a one-time gift. They kept showing up. That's a baker who comes back every single week.
Paul says it was more than once. "…you provided for my needs again and again." (Philippians 4:16). Once would've been kind. Again and again is a habit.
Paul doesn't limit it to the start. He says that even while he was in Thessalonica, "you provided for my needs again and again." (Philippians 4:16). It kept happening over time.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, "Not that I am seeking a gift, but I am looking for the fruit that may be credited to your account." (Philippians 4:17). The fruit is what he's after. The gift itself isn't the goal.

Yes, that's the flip. Paul says, "Not that I am seeking a gift, but I am looking for the fruit that may be credited to your account." (Philippians 4:17). He's not fishing for presents, friend. He's looking at what their giving grows.

True. Paul says, "I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts from Epaphroditus." (Philippians 4:18). Epaphroditus, the Philippians' messenger, brought it all the way to him. Paul's cup was full and then some.

It's actually true. Paul says, "I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts from Epaphroditus." (Philippians 4:18). Epaphroditus was the Philippians' messenger who carried them. Paul isn't just getting by, friend. He says he has more than he needs.

That's the phrase. Paul says the gifts are "a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God." (Philippians 4:18). Gifts handed to a man in chains became something pleasing to God. Your kindness is never small to Him.

A tithe is a real thing in Scripture, but it isn't Paul's word here. He calls the gifts "a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God." (Philippians 4:18). Fragrant offering is the one.

A wave offering shows up in the Law of Moses (Leviticus 7:30), but Paul doesn't use it here. He calls the gifts "a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God." (Philippians 4:18). That's the phrase to hold onto.

explanations.answer: His glorious riches in Christ Jesus
explanations.explanation: That's it. "And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:19). The measure is God's riches, not our pockets. That's a pantry with no bottom, friend.

explanations.answer: How much they have given to Paul
explanations.explanation: A nice thought, but Paul doesn't tie it to their giving. He says God will supply all their needs "according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:19). The measure is His riches, not a tally of what they gave.

Paul doesn't connect it to how faithfully they pray. He says God will supply all their needs "according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:19). The supply comes from His riches, not a score.

Yes, Caesar's household. Paul says, "All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar." (Philippians 4:22). Caesar was the Roman emperor. Saints right in that house, friend, and they're sending hello to Philippi.

explanations.answer: Those from the church in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention Jerusalem here. He says, "All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar." (Philippians 4:22). Caesar was the Roman emperor, so that's a surprising place to find saints.

explanations.answer: Those from the city of Ephesus
explanations.explanation: Ephesus isn't named in this greeting. Paul says, "All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar." (Philippians 4:22). Caesar was the Roman emperor, and his household is the one Paul points out.
